name: Drafting a Manuscript
title: Drafting a Manuscript
answer: Drafting a manuscript is the work of turning research findings into a structured document that can be submitted to a journal or conference. It covers the title, abstract, introduction, related work, methods, results, discussion, limitations, and references, along with figures, tables, and supplementary material. In AI research, the draft must also make the experimental setup, datasets, metrics, and compute reproducible enough for reviewers to assess. The draft is not the final word, it is a version that invites peer review and revision. A strong draft positions the contribution clearly against prior work and states what is new, what is uncertain, and what remains to be tested.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Drafting runs on a mix of writing tools, reference managers, and version control. Many AI researchers use LaTeX and BibTeX for typesetting and citations, while others use word processors with built in citation features. Collaborative editors and Git repositories help coauthors track changes, resolve conflicts, and keep a history of the draft. Conference and journal templates provide the required layout, word limits, and formatting rules. Compute for experiments, plotting libraries for figures, and data repositories for supplementary files are part of the same workflow.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is iterative, starting with an outline and a claim evidence table that maps each assertion to a result or citation. Authors often draft the methods and results first, then write the introduction and related work once the contribution is clear. The abstract and title are usually written last, after the main argument has settled. Coauthors circulate versions, reviewers or colleagues give feedback, and the draft is revised for clarity, consistency, and adherence to venue guidelines. Reference lists are checked against the original sources, and figures are redrawn until they stand alone without the main text.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in drafting center on authorship, citation integrity, and provenance. Authors typically agree on order and contribution, avoid plagiarism and duplicate submission, and disclose conflicts of interest, funding, and any use of AI writing tools according to venue policy. Data, code, and materials should be shared where possible, with licenses and access conditions stated clearly. Provenance means every claim and reference can be traced to a source, and that permissions for reused figures or text are in place. Breaches can lead to correction, retraction, or damage to a researcher's reputation, so journals and conferences increasingly check submissions for these issues.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Drafting is moving toward more structured, machine readable manuscripts and tighter links between text and evidence. Tools that extract claims from papers, such as the 13,608 claims in this site's library, point to a future where related work sections can be assembled from claim level data rather than prose alone. Preprint first cultures and open peer review are shortening the cycle between draft and feedback. Reproducibility checks, automated formatting, and citation validation are becoming part of the submission pipeline. The draft may increasingly be a living document that updates as new results and references appear.
sections.heading: Where it is going
